More generally, a set of eigenfunctions is also found by noting that the [differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#Differentiation) rules imply that the [ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation)      [  W  (    i  2 π      d  d x     )  + W ( x )  ]  ψ ( x ) = C ψ ( x )   {\displaystyle \left[W\left({\frac {i}{2\pi }}{\frac {d}{dx}}\right)+W(x)\right]\psi (x)=C\psi (x)}   with     C   {\displaystyle C}   constant and     W ( x )   {\displaystyle W(x)}   being a non-constant even function remains invariant in form when applying the Fourier transform       F     {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}}   to both sides of the equation. The simplest example is provided by ⁠    W ( x ) =  x  2     {\displaystyle W(x)=x^{2}}  ⁠, which is equivalent to considering the Schrödinger equation for the [quantum harmonic oscillator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_harmonic_oscillator#Natural_length_and_energy_scales).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-29) The corresponding solutions provide an important choice of an orthonormal basis for [*L*2(**R**)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-integrable_function) and are given by the "physicist's" [Hermite functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_polynomials#Hermite_functions_as_eigenfunctions_of_the_Fourier_transform). Equivalently one may use      ψ  n   ( x ) =    2  4    n !     e  − π  x  2       H e   n    (  2 x   π    )  ,   {\displaystyle \psi _{n}(x)={\frac {\sqrt[{4}]{2}}{\sqrt {n!}}}e^{-\pi x^{2}}\mathrm {He} _{n}\left(2x{\sqrt {\pi }}\right),}   where ⁠      H e   n   ( x )   {\displaystyle \mathrm {He} _{n}(x)}  ⁠ are the "probabilist's" [Hermite polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_polynomial), defined as       H e   n   ( x ) = ( − 1  )  n    e    1 2    x  2       (   d  d x    )   n    e  −   1 2    x  2     .   {\displaystyle \mathrm {He} _{n}(x)=(-1)^{n}e^{{\frac {1}{2}}x^{2}}\left({\frac {d}{dx}}\right)^{n}e^{-{\frac {1}{2}}x^{2}}.}

Under this convention for the Fourier transform, we have that         ψ ^     n   ( ξ ) = ( − i  )  n    ψ  n   ( ξ ) .   {\displaystyle {\widehat {\psi }}_{n}(\xi )=(-i)^{n}\psi _{n}(\xi ).}

In other words, the Hermite functions form a complete [orthonormal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthonormal) system of [eigenfunctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenfunctions) for the Fourier transform on ⁠     L  2   (  R  )   {\displaystyle L^{2}(\mathbb {R} )}  ⁠.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Pinsky-2002-20)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-30) However, this choice of eigenfunctions is not unique. Because of        F    4   =  i d    {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}^{4}=\mathrm {id} }   there are only four different [eigenvalues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalue) of the Fourier transform (the fourth roots of unity ⁠    ± 1   {\displaystyle \pm 1}  ⁠ and ⁠    ± i   {\displaystyle \pm i}  ⁠) and any linear combination of eigenfunctions with the same eigenvalue gives another eigenfunction.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-31) As a consequence of this, it is possible to decompose *L*2(**R**) as a direct sum of four spaces *H*0, *H*1, *H*2, and *H*3 where the Fourier transform acts on H*k* simply by multiplication by *i**k*.

Since the complete set of Hermite functions *ψn* provides a resolution of the identity they diagonalize the Fourier operator, i.e. the Fourier transform can be represented by such a sum of terms weighted by the above eigenvalues, and these sums can be explicitly summed:       F   [ f ] ( ξ ) = ∫ d x f ( x )  ∑  n ≥ 0   ( − i  )  n    ψ  n   ( x )  ψ  n   ( ξ )   .   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}[f](\xi )=\int dxf(x)\sum _{n\geq 0}(-i)^{n}\psi _{n}(x)\psi _{n}(\xi )~.}

This approach to define the Fourier transform was first proposed by [Norbert Wiener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norbert_Wiener).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Duoandikoetxea-2001-32) Among other properties, Hermite functions decrease exponentially fast in both frequency and time domains, and they are thus used to define a generalization of the Fourier transform, namely the [fractional Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_Fourier_transform) used in time–frequency analysis.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Boashash-2003-33) In [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics), this transform was introduced by [Edward Condon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Condon).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-34) This [change of basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_of_basis) becomes possible because the Fourier transform is a unitary transform when using the right [conventions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#Other_conventions). Consequently, under the proper conditions it may be expected to result from a self-adjoint generator     N   {\displaystyle N}   via[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-35)       F   [ ψ ] =  e  − i t N   ψ .   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}[\psi ]=e^{-itN}\psi .}

The operator     N   {\displaystyle N}   is the [number operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_harmonic_oscillator#Ladder_operator_method) of the quantum harmonic oscillator written as[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-auto-36)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-37)     N ≡   1  4 π     (  2 π x −   ∂  ∂ x     )   (  2 π x +   ∂  ∂ x     )  = −   1  4 π       ∂  2    ∂  x  2      + π  x  2   −   1 2   .   {\displaystyle N\equiv {\frac {1}{4\pi }}\left(2\pi x-{\frac {\partial }{\partial x}}\right)\left(2\pi x+{\frac {\partial }{\partial x}}\right)=-{\frac {1}{4\pi }}{\frac {\partial ^{2}}{\partial x^{2}}}+\pi x^{2}-{\frac {1}{2}}.}

It can be interpreted as the [generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_in_quantum_mechanics) of [fractional Fourier transforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehler_kernel#Fractional_Fourier_transform) for arbitrary values of t, and of the conventional continuous Fourier transform       F     {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}}   for the particular value ⁠    t = π  /  2   {\displaystyle t=\pi /2}  ⁠, with the [Mehler kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehler_kernel#Physics_version) implementing the corresponding [active transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_and_passive_transformation#In_abstract_vector_spaces). The eigenfunctions of     N   {\displaystyle N}   are the [Hermite functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_polynomials#Hermite_functions) ⁠     ψ  n   ( x )   {\displaystyle \psi _{n}(x)}  ⁠, which are therefore also eigenfunctions of ⁠      F     {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}}  ⁠.

Upon extending the Fourier transform to [distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_(mathematics)) the [Dirac comb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_comb#Fourier_transform) is also an eigenfunction of the Fourier transform.

Inversion and periodicity

# Inversion and periodicity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=27)] Further information: [Fourier inversion theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_inversion_theorem) and [Fractional Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_Fourier_transform)

Under suitable conditions on the function ⁠    f   {\displaystyle f}  ⁠, it can be recovered from its Fourier transform ⁠       f ^      {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}}  ⁠. Indeed, denoting the Fourier transform operator by ⁠      F     {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}}  ⁠, so ⁠      F   f :=    f ^      {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}f:={\widehat {f}}}  ⁠, then for suitable functions, applying the Fourier transform twice simply flips the function: ⁠     (     F    2   f  )  ( x ) = f ( − x )   {\displaystyle \left({\mathcal {F}}^{2}f\right)(x)=f(-x)}  ⁠, which can be interpreted as "reversing time". Since reversing time is two-periodic, applying this twice yields ⁠       F    4   ( f ) = f   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}^{4}(f)=f}  ⁠, so the Fourier transform operator is four-periodic, and similarly the inverse Fourier transform can be obtained by applying the Fourier transform three times: ⁠       F    3    (    f ^    )  = f   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}^{3}\left({\widehat {f}}\right)=f}  ⁠. In particular the Fourier transform is invertible (under suitable conditions).

More precisely, defining the *parity operator*       P     {\displaystyle {\mathcal {P}}}   such that ⁠    (   P   f ) ( x ) = f ( − x )   {\displaystyle ({\mathcal {P}}f)(x)=f(-x)}  ⁠, we have:            F    0      =  i d  ,        F    1      =   F   ,        F    2      =   P   ,        F    3      =    F    − 1   =   P   ∘   F   =   F   ∘   P   ,        F    4      =  i d        {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}{\mathcal {F}}^{0}&=\mathrm {id} ,\\{\mathcal {F}}^{1}&={\mathcal {F}},\\{\mathcal {F}}^{2}&={\mathcal {P}},\\{\mathcal {F}}^{3}&={\mathcal {F}}^{-1}={\mathcal {P}}\circ {\mathcal {F}}={\mathcal {F}}\circ {\mathcal {P}},\\{\mathcal {F}}^{4}&=\mathrm {id} \end{aligned}}}   These equalities of operators require careful definition of the space of functions in question, defining equality of functions (equality at every point? equality [almost everywhere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_everywhere)?) and defining equality of operators – that is, defining the topology on the function space and operator space in question. These are not true for all functions, but are true under various conditions, which are the content of the various forms of the [Fourier inversion theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_inversion_theorem).

This fourfold periodicity of the Fourier transform is similar to a rotation of the plane by 90°, particularly as the two-fold iteration yields a reversal, and in fact this analogy can be made precise. While the Fourier transform can simply be interpreted as switching the time domain and the frequency domain, with the inverse Fourier transform switching them back, more geometrically it can be interpreted as a rotation by 90° in the [time–frequency domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time%E2%80%93frequency_domain) (considering time as the ⁠    x   {\displaystyle x}  ⁠-axis and frequency as the ⁠    y   {\displaystyle y}  ⁠-axis), and the Fourier transform can be generalized to the [fractional Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_Fourier_transform), which involves rotations by other angles. This can be further generalized to [linear canonical transformations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_canonical_transformation), which can be visualized as the action of the [special linear group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_linear_group) [SL2(**R**)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SL2(R)) on the time–frequency plane, with the preserved symplectic form corresponding to the [uncertainty principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#Uncertainty_principle), below. This approach is particularly studied in [signal processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_processing), under [time–frequency analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time%E2%80%93frequency_analysis).

Connection with the Heisenberg group

# Connection with the Heisenberg group

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=28)]

The [Heisenberg group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heisenberg_group) is a certain [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) of [unitary operators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_operator) on the [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space) *L*2(**R**) of square integrable complex valued functions f on the real line, generated by the translations (*Ty f*)(*x*) = *f* (*x* + *y*) and multiplication by *e**i*2π*ξx*, (*Mξ f*)(*x*) = *e**i*2π*ξx* *f* (*x*). These operators do not commute, as their (group) commutator is      (   M  ξ   − 1    T  y   − 1    M  ξ    T  y   f  )  ( x ) =  e  i 2 π ξ y   f ( x ) ,   {\displaystyle \left(M_{\xi }^{-1}T_{y}^{-1}M_{\xi }T_{y}f\right)(x)=e^{i2\pi \xi y}f(x),}   which is multiplication by the constant (independent of x) *e**i*2π*ξy* ∈ *U*(1) (the [circle group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_group) of unit modulus complex numbers). As an abstract group, the Heisenberg group is the three-dimensional [Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group) of triples (*x*, *ξ*, *z*) ∈ **R**2 × *U*(1), with the group law      (   x  1   ,  ξ  1   ,  t  1    )  ⋅  (   x  2   ,  ξ  2   ,  t  2    )  =  (   x  1   +  x  2   ,  ξ  1   +  ξ  2   ,  t  1    t  2    e  − 2 i π  x  1    ξ  2      )  .   {\displaystyle \left(x_{1},\xi _{1},t_{1}\right)\cdot \left(x_{2},\xi _{2},t_{2}\right)=\left(x_{1}+x_{2},\xi _{1}+\xi _{2},t_{1}t_{2}e^{-2i\pi x_{1}\xi _{2}}\right).}

Denote the Heisenberg group by *H*1. The above procedure describes not only the group structure, but also a standard [unitary representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_representation) of *H*1 on a Hilbert space, which we denote by *ρ* : *H*1 → *B*(*L*2(**R**)). Define the linear automorphism of **R**2 by     J   (    x     ξ    )   =   (    − ξ     x    )     {\displaystyle J{\begin{pmatrix}x\\\xi \end{pmatrix}}={\begin{pmatrix}-\xi \\x\end{pmatrix}}}   so that *J*2 = −*I*. This J can be extended to a unique automorphism of *H*1:     j  (  x , ξ , t  )  =  (  − ξ , x , t  e  − i 2 π ξ x    )  .   {\displaystyle j\left(x,\xi ,t\right)=\left(-\xi ,x,te^{-i2\pi \xi x}\right).}

According to the [Stone–von Neumann theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%E2%80%93von_Neumann_theorem), the unitary representations ρ and *ρ* ∘ *j* are unitarily equivalent, so there is a unique intertwiner *W* ∈ *U*(*L*2(**R**)) such that     ρ ∘ j = W ρ  W  ∗   .   {\displaystyle \rho \circ j=W\rho W^{*}.}   This operator W is the Fourier transform.

Many of the standard properties of the Fourier transform are immediate consequences of this more general framework.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-38) For example, the square of the Fourier transform, *W*2, is an intertwiner associated with *J*2 = −*I*, and so we have (*W*2*f*)(*x*) = *f* (−*x*) is the reflection of the original function f.

Complex domain

# Complex domain

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=29)]

The [integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral) for the Fourier transform        f ^    ( ξ ) =  ∫  − ∞   ∞    e  − 2 i π t ξ   f ( t )  d t   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}(\xi )=\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }e^{-2i\pi t\xi }f(t)\,dt}   can be studied for [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) values of its argument ξ. Depending on the properties of f, this might not converge off the real axis at all, or it might converge to a [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis) [analytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_function) for all values of *ξ* = *σ* + *iτ*, or something in between.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-39)

The [Paley–Wiener theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley%E2%80%93Wiener_theorem) says that f is smooth (i.e., n-times differentiable for all positive integers n) and compactly supported if and only if *f̂* (*σ* + *iτ*) is a [holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function) for which there exists a [constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant_(mathematics)) *a* > 0 such that for any [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) *n* ≥ 0,      |   ξ  n      f ^    ( ξ )  |  ≤  C  n    e  2 π a | τ |     {\displaystyle \left\vert \xi ^{n}{\widehat {f}}(\xi )\right\vert \leq C_{n}e^{2\pi a\vert \tau \vert }}   for some constant C_n. (In this case, f is supported on [−*a*, *a*].) This can be expressed by saying that *f̂* is an [entire function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entire_function) that is [rapidly decreasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapidly_decreasing) in σ (for fixed τ) and of exponential growth in τ (uniformly in σ).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-40)

(If f is not smooth, but only *L*2, a corresponding version holds with the rapid-decrease condition replaced by the appropriate *L*2 condition.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-41)) The space of such functions of a [complex variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis) is called the Paley–Wiener space. This theorem has been generalised to semisimple [Lie groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-42)

If f is supported on the half-line *t* ≥ 0, then f is said to be "causal" because the [impulse response function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse_response_function) of a physically realisable [filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filter_(mathematics)) must have this property, as no effect can precede its cause. [Paley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Paley) and Wiener showed that then, under suitable integrability hypotheses, *f̂* extends to a [holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function) on the complex lower half-plane *τ* < 0 that tends to zero as τ goes to −∞.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-43) A simple converse in this form is false; precise converses require additional growth or Hardy-space hypotheses.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-44)

Laplace transform

# Laplace transform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=30)] See also: [Laplace transform § Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_transform#Fourier_transform)

The Fourier transform *f̂*(*ξ*) is related to the [Laplace transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_transform) *F*(*s*), which is also used for the solution of [differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_equation) and the analysis of [filters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filter_(signal_processing)).

It may happen that a function f for which the Fourier integral does not converge on the real axis at all nevertheless has a complex Fourier transform defined in some region of the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane).

For example, if f is causal and of exponential growth, i.e.,     f ( t ) = 0  ( t < 0 ) ,  | f ( t ) | < C  e  a t    ( t ≥ 0 )   {\displaystyle f(t)=0\quad (t<0),\qquad \vert f(t)\vert <Ce^{at}\quad (t\geq 0)}   for some constants *C*, *a* ≥ 0, then[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Kolmogorov-Fomin-1999-45)        f ^    ( i τ ) =  ∫  0   ∞    e  2 π τ t   f ( t )  d t ,   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}(i\tau )=\int _{0}^{\infty }e^{2\pi \tau t}f(t)\,dt,}   convergent for all 2π*τ* < −*a*, is a one-sided Laplace transform of f.

The usual one-sided version of the Laplace transform is     F ( s ) =  ∫  0   ∞   f ( t )  e  − s t    d t .   {\displaystyle F(s)=\int _{0}^{\infty }f(t)e^{-st}\,dt.}

If f is causal and the integrals converge, then ⁠       f ^    ( i τ ) = F ( − 2 π τ )   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}(i\tau )=F(-2\pi \tau )}  ⁠. Thus, extending the Fourier transform to the complex domain means it includes the Laplace transform as a special case in the case of causal functions—but with the change of variable *s* = *i*2π*ξ*.

From another, perhaps more classical viewpoint, the Laplace transform by its form involves an additional exponential regulating term that lets it converge outside of the imaginary line where the Fourier transform is defined. As such it can converge for functions and integrals with at most exponential growth in the regulated direction, whereas the original Fourier decomposition cannot, enabling analysis of systems with divergent or critical elements. Two particular examples from linear signal processing are the construction of allpass filter networks from critical comb and mitigating filters via exact pole-zero cancellation on the unit circle. Such designs are common in audio processing, where highly nonlinear [phase response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_response) is sought for, as in reverb.

Furthermore, when extended pulselike impulse responses are sought for signal processing work, the easiest way to produce them is to have one circuit that produces a divergent time response, and then to cancel its divergence through a delayed opposite and compensatory response. There, only the delay circuit in-between admits a classical Fourier description, which is critical. Both the circuits to the side are unstable, and do not admit a convergent Fourier decomposition. However, they do admit a Laplace domain description, with compatible half-planes of convergence in the complex plane (or in the discrete case, the Z-plane), wherein their effects cancel.

In modern mathematics the Laplace transform is conventionally subsumed under the aegis of Fourier methods. Both of them are subsumed by the far more general, and more abstract, idea of [harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis).

Inversion

# Inversion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=31)]

Still with ⁠    ξ = σ + i τ   {\displaystyle \xi =\sigma +i\tau }  ⁠, if        f ^      {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}}   is complex analytic for *a* ≤ *τ* ≤ *b* and has sufficient decay in horizontal strips, then      ∫  − ∞   ∞      f ^    ( σ + i a )  e  i 2 π ( σ + i a ) t    d σ =  ∫  − ∞   ∞      f ^    ( σ + i b )  e  i 2 π ( σ + i b ) t    d σ   {\displaystyle \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }{\widehat {f}}(\sigma +ia)e^{i2\pi (\sigma +ia)t}\,d\sigma =\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }{\widehat {f}}(\sigma +ib)e^{i2\pi (\sigma +ib)t}\,d\sigma }   by [Cauchy's integral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy's_integral_theorem). Therefore, the Fourier inversion formula can use integration along different lines, parallel to the real axis.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-46)

Theorem: If *f*(*t*) = 0 for *t* < 0, and |*f*(*t*)| < *Ce**at* for some constants *C*, *a* > 0 and *t* ≥ 0, then     f ( t ) =  ∫  − ∞   ∞      f ^    ( σ + i τ )  e  i 2 π ( σ + i τ ) t    d σ ,   {\displaystyle f(t)=\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }{\widehat {f}}(\sigma +i\tau )e^{i2\pi (\sigma +i\tau )t}\,d\sigma ,}   for any *τ* < −⁠*a*/2π⁠, under the usual hypotheses for Fourier inversion.

This theorem implies the [Mellin inversion formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Laplace_transform#Mellin's_inverse_formula) for the Laplace transformation,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Kolmogorov-Fomin-1999-45)     f ( t ) =   1  i 2 π     ∫  b − i ∞   b + i ∞   F ( s )  e  s t    d s   {\displaystyle f(t)={\frac {1}{i2\pi }}\int _{b-i\infty }^{b+i\infty }F(s)e^{st}\,ds}   for any *b* > *a*, where *F*(*s*) is the Laplace transform of *f*(*t*).

The hypotheses can be weakened, as in standard Fourier inversion results, to *f*(*t*) *e*−*at* being *L*1, provided that f be of [bounded variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_variation) in a closed neighborhood of t (cf. [Dini test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dini_test)), the value of f at t be taken to be the [arithmetic mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_mean) of the left and right limits, and that the integrals be taken in the sense of Cauchy principal values.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-47)

*L*2 versions of these inversion formulas are also available.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-48)

Fourier transform on Euclidean space

# Fourier transform on Euclidean space

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=32)]

The Fourier transform can be defined in any arbitrary number of dimensions n. As with the one-dimensional case, there are many conventions. For an integrable function *f*(**x**), this article takes the definition:        f ^    (  ξ  ) =   F   ( f ) (  ξ  ) =  ∫    R   n     f (  x  )  e  − i 2 π  ξ  ⋅  x     d  x    {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}({\boldsymbol {\xi }})={\mathcal {F}}(f)({\boldsymbol {\xi }})=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}f(\mathbf {x} )e^{-i2\pi {\boldsymbol {\xi }}\cdot \mathbf {x} }\,d\mathbf {x} }   where **x** and **ξ** are n-dimensional [vectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_(mathematics)), and **x** · **ξ** is the [dot product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_product) of the vectors. Alternatively, **ξ** can be viewed as belonging to the [dual vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space) ⁠      R   n ⋆     {\displaystyle \mathbb {R} ^{n\star }}  ⁠, in which case the dot product becomes the [contraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_contraction) of **x** and **ξ**, usually written as ⟨**x**, **ξ**⟩.

All of the basic properties listed above hold for the n-dimensional Fourier transform, as do Plancherel's and Parseval's theorem. When the function is integrable, the Fourier transform is still uniformly continuous and the [Riemann–Lebesgue lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Lebesgue_lemma) holds.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Stein-Weiss-1971-24)

Uncertainty principle

# Uncertainty principle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=33)] Further information: [Uncertainty principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty_principle)

Generally speaking, the more concentrated *f*(*x*) is, the more spread out its Fourier transform *f̂*(*ξ*) must be. In particular, the scaling property of the Fourier transform may be seen as saying: if we squeeze a function in x, its Fourier transform stretches out in ξ. It is not possible to arbitrarily concentrate both a function and its Fourier transform.

The trade-off between the compaction of a function and its Fourier transform can be formalized in the form of an [uncertainty principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty_principle) by viewing a function and its Fourier transform as [conjugate variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_variables) with respect to the [symplectic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_vector_space) on the [time–frequency domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time%E2%80%93frequency_representation): from the point of view of the [linear canonical transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_canonical_transformation), the Fourier transform is rotation by 90° in the time–frequency domain, and preserves the symplectic form.

Suppose *f*(*x*) is an integrable and [square-integrable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-integrable) function. [Without loss of generality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Without_loss_of_generality), assume that *f*(*x*) is normalized:      ∫  − ∞   ∞    |  f ( x )   |   2    d x = 1.   {\displaystyle \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }|f(x)|^{2}\,dx=1.}

It follows from the [Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem) that *f̂*(*ξ*) is also normalized.

The spread around *x* = 0 may be measured by the *dispersion about zero* defined by[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-49)      D  0   ( f ) =  ∫  − ∞   ∞    x  2    |  f ( x )   |   2    d x .   {\displaystyle D_{0}(f)=\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }x^{2}|f(x)|^{2}\,dx.}

In probability terms, this is the [second moment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_(mathematics)) of |*f*(*x*)|2 about zero.

The uncertainty principle states that, if *f*(*x*) is absolutely continuous and the functions *x*·*f*(*x*) and *f*′(*x*) are square integrable, then      D  0   ( f )  D  0   (    f ^    ) ≥   1  16  π  2      .   {\displaystyle D_{0}(f)D_{0}({\widehat {f}})\geq {\frac {1}{16\pi ^{2}}}.}

The equality is attained only in the case         f ( x )    =  C  1     e  − π    x  2    σ  2           ∴    f ^    ( ξ )    = σ  C  1     e  − π  σ  2    ξ  2           {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}f(x)&=C_{1}\,e^{-\pi {\frac {x^{2}}{\sigma ^{2}}}}\\\therefore {\widehat {f}}(\xi )&=\sigma C_{1}\,e^{-\pi \sigma ^{2}\xi ^{2}}\end{aligned}}}   where *σ* > 0 is arbitrary and *C*1 = ⁠4√2/√*σ*⁠ so that f is *L*2-normalized. In other words, where f is a (normalized) [Gaussian function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_function) with variance *σ*2/2π, centered at zero, and its Fourier transform is a Gaussian function with variance *σ*−2/2π. Gaussian functions are examples of [Schwartz functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_function) (see the discussion on tempered distributions below).

In fact, this inequality implies that:      (   ∫  − ∞   ∞   ( x −  x  0    )  2    |  f ( x )   |   2    d x  )   (   ∫  − ∞   ∞   ( ξ −  ξ  0    )  2     |     f ^    ( ξ )  |   2    d ξ  )  ≥   1  16  π  2      ,  ∀  x  0   ,  ξ  0   ∈  R  .   {\displaystyle \left(\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }(x-x_{0})^{2}|f(x)|^{2}\,dx\right)\left(\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }(\xi -\xi _{0})^{2}\left|{\widehat {f}}(\xi )\right|^{2}\,d\xi \right)\geq {\frac {1}{16\pi ^{2}}},\quad \forall x_{0},\xi _{0}\in \mathbb {R} .}   In [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics), the [momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum) and position [wave functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_function) are Fourier transform pairs, up to a factor of the [Planck constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planck_constant). With this constant properly taken into account, the inequality above becomes the statement of the [Heisenberg uncertainty principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heisenberg_uncertainty_principle).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-50)

A stronger uncertainty principle is the [Hirschman uncertainty principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirschman_uncertainty), which is expressed as:     H  (   | f |   2   )  + H  (   |    f ^    |   2   )  ≥ log ⁡  (   e 2   )    {\displaystyle H\left(\left|f\right|^{2}\right)+H\left(\left|{\widehat {f}}\right|^{2}\right)\geq \log \left({\frac {e}{2}}\right)}   where *H*(*p*) is the [differential entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_entropy) of the [probability density function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function) *p*(*x*):     H ( p ) = −  ∫  − ∞   ∞   p ( x ) log ⁡   (   p ( x )   )    d x   {\displaystyle H(p)=-\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }p(x)\log {\bigl (}p(x){\bigr )}\,dx}   where the logarithms may be in any base that is consistent. The equality is attained for a Gaussian, as in the previous case.

Sine and cosine transforms

# Sine and cosine transforms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=34)] Main article: [Sine and cosine transforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine_transforms)

Fourier's original formulation of the transform did not use complex numbers, but rather sines and cosines. Statisticians and others still use this form. An absolutely integrable function f for which Fourier inversion holds can be expanded in terms of genuine frequencies (avoiding negative frequencies, which are sometimes considered hard to interpret physically[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-51)) λ by     f ( t ) =  ∫  0   ∞     (   a ( λ ) cos ⁡ ( 2 π λ t ) + b ( λ ) sin ⁡ ( 2 π λ t )   )    d λ .   {\displaystyle f(t)=\int _{0}^{\infty }{\bigl (}a(\lambda )\cos(2\pi \lambda t)+b(\lambda )\sin(2\pi \lambda t){\bigr )}\,d\lambda .}

This is called an expansion as a [trigonometric integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_integral), or a Fourier integral expansion. The coefficient functions a and b can be found by using variants of the Fourier cosine transform and the Fourier sine transform (the normalisations are, again, not standardised):     a ( λ ) = 2  ∫  − ∞   ∞   f ( t ) cos ⁡ ( 2 π λ t )  d t   {\displaystyle a(\lambda )=2\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(t)\cos(2\pi \lambda t)\,dt}   and     b ( λ ) = 2  ∫  − ∞   ∞   f ( t ) sin ⁡ ( 2 π λ t )  d t .   {\displaystyle b(\lambda )=2\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(t)\sin(2\pi \lambda t)\,dt.}

Older literature refers to the two transform functions, the Fourier cosine transform, a, and the Fourier sine transform, b.

The function f can be recovered from the sine and cosine transform using     f ( t ) = 2  ∫  0   ∞    ∫  − ∞   ∞   f ( τ ) cos ⁡   (   2 π λ ( τ − t )   )    d τ  d λ .   {\displaystyle f(t)=2\int _{0}^{\infty }\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(\tau )\cos {\bigl (}2\pi \lambda (\tau -t){\bigr )}\,d\tau \,d\lambda .}   together with trigonometric identities. This is referred to as Fourier's integral formula.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Kolmogorov-Fomin-1999-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-52)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-53)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-54)

Spherical harmonics

# Spherical harmonics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=35)]

Let the set of [homogeneous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_polynomial) [harmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_function) [polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) of degree k on **R***n* be denoted by **A***k*. The set **A***k* consists of the [solid spherical harmonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_spherical_harmonics) of degree k. The solid spherical harmonics play a similar role in higher dimensions to the Hermite polynomials in dimension one. Specifically, if *f*(*x*) = *e*−π|*x*|2*P*(*x*) for some *P*(*x*) in **A***k*, then ⁠       f ^    ( ξ ) =  i  − k   f ( ξ )   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}(\xi )=i^{-k}f(\xi )}  ⁠. Let the set **H***k* be the closure in *L*2(**R***n*) of linear combinations of functions of the form *f*(|*x*|)*P*(*x*) where *P*(*x*) is in **A***k*. The space *L*2(**R***n*) is then a direct sum of the spaces **H***k* and the Fourier transform maps each space **H***k* to itself and it is possible to characterize the action of the Fourier transform on each space **H***k*.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Stein-Weiss-1971-24)

Let *f*(*x*) = *f*0(|*x*|)*P*(*x*) (with *P*(*x*) in **A***k*), then        f ^    ( ξ ) =  F  0   (  |  ξ  |  ) P ( ξ )   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}(\xi )=F_{0}(|\xi |)P(\xi )}   where      F  0   ( r ) = 2 π  i  − k    r  −    n + 2 k − 2  2      ∫  0   ∞    f  0   ( s )  J    n + 2 k − 2  2    ( 2 π r s )  s    n + 2 k  2     d s .   {\displaystyle F_{0}(r)=2\pi i^{-k}r^{-{\frac {n+2k-2}{2}}}\int _{0}^{\infty }f_{0}(s)J_{\frac {n+2k-2}{2}}(2\pi rs)s^{\frac {n+2k}{2}}\,ds.}

Here *J*(*n* + 2*k* − 2)/2 denotes the [Bessel function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessel_function) of the first kind with order ⁠*n* + 2*k* − 2/2⁠. When *k* = 0 this gives a useful formula for the Fourier transform of a radial function.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-55) This is essentially the [Hankel transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hankel_transform). Moreover, there is a simple recursion relating the cases *n* + 2 and n[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-56) allowing to compute, e.g., the three-dimensional Fourier transform of a radial function from the one-dimensional one.

Restriction problems

# Restriction problems

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=36)] See also: [Fourier extension operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_extension_operator)

In higher dimensions it becomes interesting to study *restriction problems* for the Fourier transform. The Fourier transform of an integrable function is continuous and the restriction of this function to any set is defined. But for a square-integrable function the Fourier transform could be a general *class* of square integrable functions. As such, the restriction of the Fourier transform of an *L*2(**R***n*) function cannot be defined on sets of measure 0. It is still an active area of study to understand restriction problems in *L**p* for 1 < *p* < 2. It is possible in some cases to define the restriction of a Fourier transform to a set S, provided S has non-zero curvature. The case when S is the unit sphere in **R***n* is of particular interest. In this case the Tomas–[Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Stein) restriction theorem states that the restriction of the Fourier transform to the unit sphere in **R***n* is a bounded operator on *L**p* provided 1 ≤ *p* ≤ ⁠2*n* + 2/*n* + 3⁠.

One notable difference between the Fourier transform in 1 dimension versus higher dimensions concerns the partial sum operator. Consider an increasing collection of measurable sets *E**R* indexed by *R* ∈ (0, ∞): such as balls of radius R centered at the origin, or cubes of side 2*R*. For a given integrable function f, consider the function fR defined by:      f  R   ( x ) =  ∫   E  R        f ^    ( ξ )  e  i 2 π x ⋅ ξ    d ξ ,  x ∈   R   n   .   {\displaystyle f_{R}(x)=\int _{E_{R}}{\widehat {f}}(\xi )e^{i2\pi x\cdot \xi }\,d\xi ,\quad x\in \mathbb {R} ^{n}.}

Suppose in addition that *f* ∈ *L**p*(**R***n*). For *n* = 1 and 1 < *p* < ∞, if one takes *ER* = (−*R*, *R*), then fR converges to f in *L**p* as R tends to infinity, by the boundedness of the [Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform). Naively one may hope the same holds true for *n* > 1. In the case that ER is taken to be a cube with side length R, then convergence still holds. Another natural candidate is the Euclidean ball *E**R* = {*ξ* : |*ξ*| < *R*}. In order for this partial sum operator to converge, it is necessary that the [multiplier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplier_(Fourier_analysis)) for the unit ball be bounded in *L**p*(**R***n*). For *n* ≥ 2 it is a celebrated theorem of [Charles Fefferman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Fefferman) that the multiplier for the unit ball is never bounded unless *p* = 2.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-57) In fact, when *p* ≠ 2, this shows that not only may fR fail to converge to f in *L**p*, but for some functions *f* ∈ *L**p*(**R***n*), fR is not even an element of *L**p*.

Fourier transform on function spaces

# Fourier transform on function spaces

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=37)] See also: [Riesz–Thorin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Thorin_theorem)

The definition of the Fourier transform naturally extends from      L  1   (  R  )   {\displaystyle L^{1}(\mathbb {R} )}   to ⁠     L  1   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle L^{1}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}  ⁠. That is, if     f ∈  L  1   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle f\in L^{1}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   then the Fourier transform       F   :  L  1   (   R   n   ) →  L  ∞   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}:L^{1}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})\to L^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   is given by     f ( x ) ↦    f ^    ( ξ ) =  ∫    R   n     f ( x )  e  − i 2 π ξ ⋅ x    d x ,  ∀ ξ ∈   R   n   .   {\displaystyle f(x)\mapsto {\widehat {f}}(\xi )=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}f(x)e^{-i2\pi \xi \cdot x}\,dx,\quad \forall \xi \in \mathbb {R} ^{n}.}   This operator is [bounded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_operator) as      sup  ξ ∈   R   n      |     f ^    ( ξ )  |  ≤  ∫    R   n     | f ( x ) |  d x ,   {\displaystyle \sup _{\xi \in \mathbb {R} ^{n}}\left\vert {\widehat {f}}(\xi )\right\vert \leq \int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}\vert f(x)\vert \,dx,}   which shows that its [operator norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_norm) is bounded by 1. The [Riemann–Lebesgue lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Lebesgue_lemma) shows that if     f ∈  L  1   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle f\in L^{1}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   then its Fourier transform actually belongs to the [space of continuous functions that vanish at infinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_space#Functional_analysis), i.e., ⁠       f ^    ∈  C  0   (   R   n   ) ⊂  L  ∞   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}\in C_{0}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})\subset L^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}  ⁠.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTESteinWeiss19711%E2%80%932-58)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTERudin1987182%E2%80%93183-59) Furthermore, the [image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_(mathematics)) of      L  1     {\displaystyle L^{1}}   under       F     {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}}   is a strict subset of ⁠     C  0   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle C_{0}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}  ⁠.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChandrasekharan19897%E2%80%938,_84-60)

Similarly to the case of one variable, the Fourier transform can be defined on ⁠     L  2   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle L^{2}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}  ⁠. The Fourier transform in      L  2   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle L^{2}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   is no longer given by an ordinary Lebesgue integral, although it can be computed by an [improper integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improper_integral), i.e.,        f ^    ( ξ ) =  lim  R → ∞    ∫   |  x  |  ≤ R   f ( x )  e  − i 2 π ξ ⋅ x    d x   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}(\xi )=\lim _{R\to \infty }\int _{|x|\leq R}f(x)e^{-i2\pi \xi \cdot x}\,dx}   where the limit is taken in the *L*2 sense.[[note 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-61)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-62)

Furthermore,       F   :  L  2   (   R   n   ) →  L  2   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}:L^{2}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})\to L^{2}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   is a [unitary operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_operator).[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTESteinWeiss1971Thm._2.3-63) For an operator to be unitary it is sufficient to show that it is bijective and preserves the inner product. The Fourier inversion theorem implies that the transform is bijective. Also, for any *f*, *g* ∈ *L*2(**R***n*) we have      ∫    R   n     f ( x )   F   g ( x )  d x =  ∫    R   n       F   f ( x ) g ( x )  d x .   {\displaystyle \int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}f(x){\mathcal {F}}g(x)\,dx=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}{\mathcal {F}}f(x)g(x)\,dx.}   So          ∫    R   n          F   f ( x )  ¯     F   g ( x )  d x    =  ∫    R   n        F    − 1      f ( x )  ¯     F   g ( x )  d x       =  ∫    R   n       F      F    − 1      f ( x )  ¯   g ( x )  d x =  ∫    R   n        f ( x )  ¯   g ( x )  d x       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}{\overline {{\mathcal {F}}f(x)}}{\mathcal {F}}g(x)\,dx&=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}{\mathcal {F}}^{-1}{\overline {f(x)}}{\mathcal {F}}g(x)\,dx\\&=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}{\mathcal {F}}{\mathcal {F}}^{-1}{\overline {f(x)}}g(x)\,dx=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}{\overline {f(x)}}g(x)\,dx\end{aligned}}}

So the transform preserves the inner product.

On other *L**p*

# On other *L**p*

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=38)]

For ⁠    1 < p < 2   {\displaystyle 1<p<2}  ⁠, the Fourier transform can be defined on      L  p   (  R  )   {\displaystyle L^{p}(\mathbb {R} )}   by [Riesz–Thorin interpolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Thorin_interpolation?action=edit&redlink=1), which amounts to decomposing such functions into a fat tail part      |  f  |  ≤ 1   {\displaystyle |f|\leq 1}   in *L*2 plus a fat body part      |  f  |  > 1   {\displaystyle |f|>1}   in *L*1. In each of these spaces, the Fourier transform of a function in *L**p*(**R***n*) is in *L**q*(**R***n*), where *q* = ⁠*p*/*p* − 1⁠ is the [Hölder conjugate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B6lder_conjugate) of p (by the [Hausdorff–Young inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff%E2%80%93Young_inequality)). However, except for *p* = 2, the image is not easily characterized. Further extensions become more technical. The Fourier transform of functions in *L**p* for the range 2 < *p* < ∞ requires the study of distributions.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKatznelson2004-64) In fact, it can be shown that there are functions in *L**p* with *p* > 2 so that the Fourier transform is not defined as a function.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Stein-Weiss-1971-24)

Tempered distributions

# Tempered distributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=39)] Main article: [Distribution (mathematics) § Tempered distributions and Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_(mathematics)#Tempered_distributions_and_Fourier_transform) See also: [Rigged Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigged_Hilbert_space)

One might consider enlarging the domain of the Fourier transform from      L  1   +  L  2     {\displaystyle L^{1}+L^{2}}   by considering [generalized functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_function), or distributions. A distribution on       R   n     {\displaystyle \mathbb {R} ^{n}}   is a continuous linear functional on the space      C  c   ∞   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   of compactly supported smooth functions (i.e. [bump functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bump_function)), equipped with a suitable topology. Since      C  c   ∞   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   is dense in ⁠     L  2   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle L^{2}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}  ⁠, the [Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem) allows one to extend the definition of the Fourier transform to general functions in      L  2   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle L^{2}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   by continuity arguments. The strategy is then to consider the action of the Fourier transform on      C  c   ∞   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   and pass to distributions by duality. The obstruction to doing this is that the Fourier transform does not map      C  c   ∞   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   to ⁠     C  c   ∞   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}  ⁠. In fact the Fourier transform of an element in      C  c   ∞   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   can not vanish on an open set; see the above discussion on the uncertainty principle.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMallat200945-65)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStrichartz1994150-66)

The Fourier transform can also be defined for [tempered distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempered_distribution) ⁠       S   ′  (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {S}}'(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}  ⁠, dual to the space of [Schwartz functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_function) ⁠      S   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {S}}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}  ⁠. A Schwartz function is a smooth function that decays at infinity, along with all of its derivatives, hence      C  c   ∞   (   R   n   ) ⊂   S   (   R   n   )   {\displaystyle C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})\subset {\mathcal {S}}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})}   and:       F   :  C  c   ∞   (   R   n   ) →   S   (   R   n   ) ∖  C  c   ∞   (   R   n   ) .   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {F}}:C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n})\rightarrow {\mathcal {S}}(\mathbb {R} ^{n})\setminus C_{c}^{\infty }(\mathbb {R} ^{n}).}   The Fourier transform is an [automorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism) of the Schwartz space and, by duality, also an automorphism of the space of tempered distributions.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Stein-Weiss-1971-24)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2014-67) The tempered distributions include well-behaved functions of polynomial growth, distributions of compact support as well as all the integrable functions mentioned above.

For the definition of the Fourier transform of a tempered distribution, let     f   {\displaystyle f}   and     g   {\displaystyle g}   be integrable functions, and let        f ^      {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}}   and        g ^      {\displaystyle {\widehat {g}}}   be their Fourier transforms respectively. Then the Fourier transform obeys the following multiplication formula,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Stein-Weiss-1971-24)      ∫    R   n        f ^    ( x ) g ( x )  d x =  ∫    R   n     f ( x )    g ^    ( x )  d x .   {\displaystyle \int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}{\widehat {f}}(x)g(x)\,dx=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}f(x){\widehat {g}}(x)\,dx.}

Every integrable function     f   {\displaystyle f}   defines (induces) a distribution      T  f     {\displaystyle T_{f}}   by the relation      T  f   ( φ ) =  ∫    R   n     f ( x ) φ ( x )  d x ,  ∀ φ ∈   S   (   R   n   ) .   {\displaystyle T_{f}(\varphi )=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}f(x)\varphi (x)\,dx,\quad \forall \varphi \in {\mathcal {S}}(\mathbb {R} ^{n}).}   So it makes sense to define the Fourier transform of a tempered distribution      T  f   ∈    S   ′  (  R  )   {\displaystyle T_{f}\in {\mathcal {S}}'(\mathbb {R} )}   by the duality:     ⟨     T ^     f   , φ ⟩ = ⟨  T  f   ,    φ ^    ⟩ ,  ∀ φ ∈   S   (   R   n   ) .   {\displaystyle \langle {\widehat {T}}_{f},\varphi \rangle =\langle T_{f},{\widehat {\varphi }}\rangle ,\quad \forall \varphi \in {\mathcal {S}}(\mathbb {R} ^{n}).}   Extending this to all tempered distributions     T   {\displaystyle T}   gives the general definition of the Fourier transform.

Distributions can be differentiated and the above-mentioned compatibility of the Fourier transform with differentiation and convolution remains true for tempered distributions.

Generalizations

# Generalizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=40)]

Fourier–Stieltjes transform on measurable spaces

# Fourier–Stieltjes transform on measurable spaces

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=41)] See also: [Bochner–Minlos theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Minlos_theorem), [Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem), and [Fourier series § Fourier-Stieltjes series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series#Fourier-Stieltjes_series)

The Fourier transform of a [finite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_measure) [Borel measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_measure) μ on **R***n*, given by the bounded, uniformly continuous function:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPinsky2002256-68)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTERudin199115-69)        μ ^    ( ξ ) =  ∫    R   n      e  − i 2 π x ⋅ ξ    d μ ,   {\displaystyle {\widehat {\mu }}(\xi )=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{n}}e^{-i2\pi x\cdot \xi }\,d\mu ,}   is called the *Fourier–Stieltjes transform* due to its connection with the [Riemann-Stieltjes integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Stieltjes_integral#Application_to_functional_analysis) representation of [(Radon) measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_measure).[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwards198253,_67,_72%E2%80%9373-70) If     μ   {\displaystyle \mu }   is the [probability distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution) of a [random variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_variable)     X   {\displaystyle X}   then its Fourier–Stieltjes transform is, by definition, a [characteristic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_function_(probability_theory)).[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-71) If, in addition, the probability distribution has a [probability density function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function), this definition is subject to the usual Fourier transform.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBillingsley1995345-72) Stated more generally, when     μ   {\displaystyle \mu }   is [absolutely continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_continuity#Absolute_continuity_of_measures) with respect to the Lebesgue measure, i.e.,     d μ = f ( x )  d x ,   {\displaystyle d\mu =f(x)\,dx,}   then        μ ^    ( ξ ) =    f ^    ( ξ ) ,   {\displaystyle {\widehat {\mu }}(\xi )={\widehat {f}}(\xi ),}   and the Fourier-Stieltjes transform reduces to the usual definition of the Fourier transform. That is, the notable difference with the Fourier transform of integrable functions is that the Fourier-Stieltjes transform need not vanish at infinity, i.e., the [Riemann–Lebesgue lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Lebesgue_lemma) fails for measures.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKatznelson200440,_155,_164-73)

[Bochner's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner's_theorem) characterizes which functions may arise as the Fourier–Stieltjes transform of a positive measure on the circle.

One example of a finite Borel measure that is not a function is the [Dirac measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_measure).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwards198253-74) Its Fourier transform is a constant function (whose value depends on the form of the Fourier transform used).

Locally compact abelian groups

# Locally compact abelian groups

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=42)] Main article: [Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)

The Fourier transform may be generalized to any [locally compact abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_compact_abelian_group), i.e., an [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group) that is also a [locally compact Hausdorff space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_compact_Hausdorff_space) such that the group operation is continuous. If G is a locally compact abelian group, it has a translation invariant measure μ, called [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). For a locally compact abelian group G, the set of irreducible, i.e. one-dimensional, unitary representations are called its [characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_group). With its natural group structure and the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets (that is, the topology induced by the [compact-open topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact-open_topology) on the space of all continuous functions from     G   {\displaystyle G}   to the [circle group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_group)), the set of characters Ĝ is itself a locally compact abelian group, called the *Pontryagin dual* of G. For a function f in *L*1(*G*), its Fourier transform is defined by[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKatznelson2004-64)        f ^    ( ξ ) =  ∫  G      ξ ( x )  ¯   f ( x )  d μ   for any   ξ ∈    G ^    .   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}(\xi )=\int _{G}{\overline {\xi (x)}}f(x)\,d\mu \quad {\text{for any }}\xi \in {\widehat {G}}.}

The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma holds in this case; *f̂*(*ξ*) is a function vanishing at infinity on Ĝ.

The Fourier transform on T = R/Z is an example; here T is a locally compact abelian group, and the Haar measure μ on T can be thought of as the Lebesgue measure on [0,1). Consider a representation of T on the complex plane C thought of as a 1-dimensional complex vector space. There is a group of such representations (which are irreducible since C is 1-dim)     {  e  k   : T → G  L  1   ( C ) =  C  ∗   ∣ k ∈ Z }   {\displaystyle \{e_{k}:T\rightarrow GL_{1}(C)=C^{*}\mid k\in Z\}}   where      e  k   ( x ) =  e  i 2 π k x     {\displaystyle e_{k}(x)=e^{i2\pi kx}}   for ⁠    x ∈ T   {\displaystyle x\in T}  ⁠.

The character of such representation, that is the trace of      e  k   ( x )   {\displaystyle e_{k}(x)}   (thought of as a one-by-one matrix) for each     x ∈ T   {\displaystyle x\in T}   and ⁠    k ∈ Z   {\displaystyle k\in Z}  ⁠, is      e  i 2 π k x     {\displaystyle e^{i2\pi kx}}   itself. Now, in the case of representations of finite groups, the character table of a group G consists of rows of vectors such that each row is the character of one irreducible representation of G, and these vectors form an orthonormal basis of the space of class (meaning conjugation-invariant) functions that map from G to C by Schur's lemma. The group T is no longer finite but still compact, and it preserves the orthonormality of the character table. Each row of the table is the function      e  k   ( x )   {\displaystyle e_{k}(x)}   of ⁠    x ∈ T   {\displaystyle x\in T}  ⁠, and the inner product between two class functions (all functions being class functions since T is abelian)     f , g ∈  L  2   ( T , d μ )   {\displaystyle f,g\in L^{2}(T,d\mu )}   is defined as     ⟨ f , g ⟩ =   1   |  T  |      ∫  [ 0 , 1 )   f ( y )   g ¯   ( y ) d μ ( y )   {\textstyle \langle f,g\rangle ={\frac {1}{|T|}}\int _{[0,1)}f(y){\overline {g}}(y)d\mu (y)}   with the normalizing factor ⁠    | T | = 1   {\displaystyle \vert T\vert =1}  ⁠. The sequence     {  e  k   ∣ k ∈ Z }   {\displaystyle \{e_{k}\mid k\in Z\}}   is an orthonormal basis of the space of class functions ⁠     L  2   ( T , d μ )   {\displaystyle L^{2}(T,d\mu )}  ⁠.

For any representation V of a finite group G,      χ  v     {\displaystyle \chi _{v}}   can be expressed as the span      ∑  i    ⟨   χ  v   ,  χ   v  i      ⟩   χ   v  i       {\textstyle \sum _{i}\left\langle \chi _{v},\chi _{v_{i}}\right\rangle \chi _{v_{i}}}   (     V  i     {\displaystyle V_{i}}   are the irreducible representations of G), such that ⁠      ⟨   χ  v   ,  χ   v  i      ⟩  =   1  | G |     ∑  g ∈ G    χ  v   ( g )    χ ¯     v  i     ( g )    {\displaystyle \textstyle \left\langle \chi _{v},\chi _{v_{i}}\right\rangle ={\frac {1}{\vert G\vert }}\sum _{g\in G}\chi _{v}(g){\overline {\chi }}_{v_{i}}(g)}  ⁠. Similarly for     G = T   {\displaystyle G=T}   and ⁠    f ∈  L  2   ( T , d μ )   {\displaystyle f\in L^{2}(T,d\mu )}  ⁠, ⁠     f ( x ) =  ∑  k ∈ Z      f ^    ( k )  e  k      {\displaystyle \textstyle f(x)=\sum _{k\in Z}{\widehat {f}}(k)e_{k}}  ⁠. The Pontriagin dual        T ^      {\displaystyle {\widehat {T}}}   is     {  e  k   } ( k ∈ Z )   {\displaystyle \{e_{k}\}(k\in Z)}   and for ⁠    f ∈  L  2   ( T , d μ )   {\displaystyle f\in L^{2}(T,d\mu )}  ⁠,        f ^    ( k ) =   1   |  T  |      ∫  [ 0 , 1 )   f ( y )  e  − i 2 π k y   d y   {\textstyle {\widehat {f}}(k)={\frac {1}{|T|}}\int _{[0,1)}f(y)e^{-i2\pi ky}dy}   is its Fourier transform for ⁠     e  k   ∈    T ^      {\displaystyle e_{k}\in {\widehat {T}}}  ⁠.

Gelfand transform

# Gelfand transform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=43)] Main article: [Gelfand representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation)

The Fourier transform is also a special case of the [Gelfand transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_transform). In this particular context, it is closely related to the Pontryagin duality map defined above.

Given an abelian [locally compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_compact_space) [Hausdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_space) [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group) G, as before we consider the space *L*1(*G*), defined using a Haar measure. With convolution as multiplication, *L*1(*G*) is an abelian [Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra). It also has an [involution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Involution_(mathematics)) * given by      f  ∗   ( g ) =    f  (  g  − 1   )   ¯   .   {\displaystyle f^{*}(g)={\overline {f\left(g^{-1}\right)}}.}

Taking the completion with respect to the largest possible *C**-norm gives its enveloping *C**-algebra, called the group *C**-algebra *C**(*G*) of G. (Any *C**-norm on *L*1(*G*) is bounded by the *L*1 norm, therefore their supremum exists.)

Given any abelian *C**-algebra A, the Gelfand transform gives an isomorphism between A and *C*0(*A*^), where *A*^ is the multiplicative linear functionals, i.e. one-dimensional representations, on A with the weak-* topology. The map is simply given by     a ↦   (   φ ↦ φ ( a )   )   .   {\displaystyle a\mapsto {\bigl (}\varphi \mapsto \varphi (a){\bigr )}.}   It turns out that the multiplicative linear functionals of *C**(*G*), after suitable identification, are exactly the characters of G, and the Gelfand transform, when restricted to the dense subset *L*1(*G*), is the Fourier–Pontryagin transform.

Compact non-abelian groups

# Compact non-abelian groups

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=44)]

The Fourier transform can also be defined for functions on a non-abelian group, provided that the group is [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space). Removing the assumption that the underlying group is abelian, irreducible unitary representations need not always be one-dimensional. This means the Fourier transform on a non-abelian group takes values as Hilbert space operators.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-75) The Fourier transform on compact groups is a major tool in [representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-76) and [non-commutative harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-commutative_harmonic_analysis).

Let G be a compact [Hausdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_space) [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group), and let λ be its normalized [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). Let Σ denote the collection of all isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional irreducible [unitary representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_representation), along with a definite choice of representation *U*(*σ*) on the [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space) *Hσ* of finite dimension *dσ* for each *σ* ∈ Σ.

For *f* ∈ *L*1(*G*), the Fourier transform of f at σ is the operator on *Hσ* defined by        f ^    ( σ ) =  ∫  G   f ( g )  U   g  − 1     ( σ )    d λ ( g ) .   {\displaystyle {\widehat {f}}(\sigma )=\int _{G}f(g)U_{g^{-1}}^{(\sigma )}\,d\lambda (g).}   Equivalently,       ⟨     f ^    ( σ ) ξ , η  ⟩    H  σ     =  ∫  G   f ( g )  ⟨   U   g  − 1     ( σ )   ξ , η  ⟩   d λ ( g ) .   {\displaystyle \left\langle {\widehat {f}}(\sigma )\xi ,\eta \right\rangle _{H_{\sigma }}=\int _{G}f(g)\left\langle U_{g^{-1}}^{(\sigma )}\xi ,\eta \right\rangle \,d\lambda (g).}   Since *U*(*σ*) is unitary, this may also be written using the adjoint        U  ( σ )     g   ∗     {\displaystyle {U^{(\sigma )}}_{g}^{*}}  .

If μ is a finite complex [Borel measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_measure) on G, then the Fourier–Stieltjes transform of μ is the operator on *Hσ* defined by        μ ^    ( σ ) =  ∫  G    U   g  − 1     ( σ )    d μ ( g ) ,   {\displaystyle {\widehat {\mu }}(\sigma )=\int _{G}U_{g^{-1}}^{(\sigma )}\,d\mu (g),}   or, weakly,       ⟨     μ ^    ( σ ) ξ , η  ⟩    H  σ     =  ∫  G    ⟨   U   g  − 1     ( σ )   ξ , η  ⟩   d μ ( g ) .   {\displaystyle \left\langle {\widehat {\mu }}(\sigma )\xi ,\eta \right\rangle _{H_{\sigma }}=\int _{G}\left\langle U_{g^{-1}}^{(\sigma )}\xi ,\eta \right\rangle \,d\mu (g).}   If μ is [absolutely continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolutely_continuous) with respect to λ, [represented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym_theorem) as     d μ = f  d λ   {\displaystyle d\mu =f\,d\lambda }   for some *f* ∈ [*L*1(*G*)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space), one identifies the Fourier transform of f with the Fourier–Stieltjes transform of μ.

The mapping     μ ↦    μ ^      {\displaystyle \mu \mapsto {\widehat {\mu }}}   is injective and sends finite measures to bounded fields of operators (\widehat\mu(\sigma))σ∈Σ, with      sup  σ ∈ Σ   ‖    μ ^    ( σ ) ‖ ≤ ‖ μ ‖ .   {\displaystyle \sup _{\sigma \in \Sigma }\|{\widehat {\mu }}(\sigma )\|\leq \|\mu \|.}   Thus it may be viewed as a representation of the [Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra) *M*(*G*) of finite Borel measures, with multiplication given by [convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution) of measures. With the convention above, convolution corresponds to operator multiplication with the order reversed:         μ ∗ ν  ^    ( σ ) =    ν ^    ( σ )    μ ^    ( σ ) .   {\displaystyle {\widehat {\mu *\nu }}(\sigma )={\widehat {\nu }}(\sigma ){\widehat {\mu }}(\sigma ).}   Using the alternative convention \widehat f(\sigma)=\int_G f(g)U^{(\sigma)}_g\,d\lambda(g) reverses this order. The involution on *M*(*G*) is given, for absolutely continuous measures, by      f  ∗   ( g ) =    f (  g  − 1   )  ¯   ,   {\displaystyle f^{*}(g)={\overline {f(g^{-1})}},}   since compact groups are unimodular.

The [Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem) holds, and a version of the Fourier inversion formula follows: if *f* ∈ *L*2(*G*), then     f ( g ) =  ∑  σ ∈ Σ    d  σ   tr ⁡  (     f ^    ( σ )  U  g   ( σ )    )  ,   {\displaystyle f(g)=\sum _{\sigma \in \Sigma }d_{\sigma }\operatorname {tr} \left({\widehat {f}}(\sigma )U_{g}^{(\sigma )}\right),}   where the summation is understood as convergent in the *L*2 sense. The corresponding Plancherel formula is     ‖ f  ‖  2   2   =  ∑  σ ∈ Σ    d  σ   ‖    f ^    ( σ )  ‖   H S    2   ,   {\displaystyle \|f\|_{2}^{2}=\sum _{\sigma \in \Sigma }d_{\sigma }\|{\widehat {f}}(\sigma )\|_{\mathrm {HS} }^{2},}   where ||·||HS denotes the [Hilbert–Schmidt norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_operator).

The generalization of the Fourier transform to the noncommutative situation has also in part contributed to the development of [noncommutative geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noncommutative_geometry).[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*] In this context, a categorical generalization of the Fourier transform to noncommutative groups is [Tannaka–Krein duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannaka%E2%80%93Krein_duality), which replaces the group of characters with the category of representations. However, this is no longer simply a transform of scalar-valued functions into scalar-valued functions.

Alternatives

# Alternatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=45)]

In [signal processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_processing) terms, a function (of time) is a representation of a signal with perfect *time resolution*, but no frequency information, while the Fourier transform has perfect *frequency resolution*, but no time information: the magnitude of the Fourier transform at a point is how much frequency content there is, but location is only given by phase (argument of the Fourier transform at a point), and [standing waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_wave) are not localized in time – a sine wave continues out to infinity, without decaying. This limits the usefulness of the Fourier transform for analyzing signals that are localized in time, notably [transients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transient_(acoustics)), or any signal of finite extent.

As alternatives to the Fourier transform, in [time–frequency analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time%E2%80%93frequency_analysis), one uses time–frequency transforms or time–frequency distributions to represent signals in a form that has some time information and some frequency information – by the uncertainty principle, there is a trade-off between these. These can be generalizations of the Fourier transform, such as the [short-time Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-time_Fourier_transform), [fractional Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_Fourier_transform), synchrosqueezing Fourier transform,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-FOOTNOTECorreiaJustoAng%C3%A9lico2024-77) or other functions to represent signals, as in [wavelet transforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelet_transform) and [chirplet transforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirplet_transform), with the wavelet analog of the Fourier transform being the [continuous wavelet transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_wavelet_transform).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-Boashash-2003-33)

Example

# Example

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=46)]

The following figures provide a visual illustration of how the Fourier transform's integral measures whether a frequency is present in a particular function. The first image depicts the function ⁠    f ( t ) = cos ⁡ ( 2 π   3 t )    e  − π  t  2       {\displaystyle f(t)=\cos(2\pi \ 3t)\ e^{-\pi t^{2}}}  ⁠, which is a 3 [Hz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertz) cosine wave (the first term) shaped by a [Gaussian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_function) [envelope function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(waves)) (the second term) that smoothly turns the wave on and off. The next 2 images show the product ⁠    f ( t )  e  − i 2 π 3 t     {\displaystyle f(t)e^{-i2\pi 3t}}  ⁠, which must be integrated to calculate the Fourier transform at +3 Hz. The real part of the integrand has a non-negative average value, because the alternating signs of     f ( t )   {\displaystyle f(t)}   and     Re ⁡ (  e  − i 2 π 3 t   )   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (e^{-i2\pi 3t})}   oscillate at the same rate and in phase, whereas     f ( t )   {\displaystyle f(t)}   and     Im ⁡ (  e  − i 2 π 3 t   )   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Im} (e^{-i2\pi 3t})}   oscillate at the same rate but with orthogonal phase. The absolute value of the Fourier transform at +3 Hz is 0.5, which is relatively large. When added to the Fourier transform at −3 Hz (which is identical because we started with a real signal), we find that the amplitude of the 3 Hz frequency component is 1.

 [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Onfreq.png/960px-Onfreq.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Onfreq.png)Original function, which has a strong 3 Hz component. Real and imaginary parts of the integrand of its Fourier transform at +3 Hz.

However, when you try to measure a frequency that is not present, both the real and imaginary component of the integral vary rapidly between positive and negative values. For instance, the red curve is looking for 5 Hz. The absolute value of its integral is nearly zero, indicating that almost no 5 Hz component was in the signal. The general situation is usually more complicated than this, but heuristically this is how the Fourier transform measures how much of an individual frequency is present in a function ⁠    f ( t )   {\displaystyle f(t)}  ⁠.

- [![Real and imaginary parts of the integrand for its Fourier transform at \+5 Hz\.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Offfreq_i2p.svg/500px-Offfreq_i2p.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Offfreq_i2p.svg) Real and imaginary parts of the integrand for its Fourier transform at +5 Hz.
- [![Magnitude of its Fourier transform, with \+3 and \+5 Hz labeled\.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Fourier_transform_of_oscillating_function.svg/500px-Fourier_transform_of_oscillating_function.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fourier_transform_of_oscillating_function.svg) Magnitude of its Fourier transform, with +3 and +5 Hz labeled.

To re-enforce an earlier point, the reason for the response at     ξ = − 3   {\displaystyle \xi =-3}   Hz is because     cos ⁡ ( 2 π 3 t )   {\displaystyle \cos(2\pi 3t)}   and     cos ⁡ ( 2 π ( − 3 ) t )   {\displaystyle \cos(2\pi (-3)t)}   are indistinguishable. The transform of      e  i 2 π 3 t   ⋅  e  − π  t  2       {\displaystyle e^{i2\pi 3t}\cdot e^{-\pi t^{2}}}   would have just one response, whose amplitude is the integral of the smooth envelope: ⁠     e  − π  t  2       {\displaystyle e^{-\pi t^{2}}}  ⁠, whereas     Re ⁡ ( f ( t ) ⋅  e  − i 2 π 3 t   )   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (f(t)\cdot e^{-i2\pi 3t})}   is ⁠     e  − π  t  2     ( 1 + cos ⁡ ( 2 π 6 t ) )  /  2   {\displaystyle e^{-\pi t^{2}}(1+\cos(2\pi 6t))/2}  ⁠.

Applications

# Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=47)] See also: [Spectral density § Applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_density#Applications) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Commutative_diagram_illustrating_problem_solving_via_the_Fourier_transform.svg/500px-Commutative_diagram_illustrating_problem_solving_via_the_Fourier_transform.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commutative_diagram_illustrating_problem_solving_via_the_Fourier_transform.svg)Some problems, such as certain differential equations, become easier to solve when the Fourier transform is applied. In that case the solution to the original problem is recovered using the inverse Fourier transform.

Linear operations performed in one domain (time or frequency) have corresponding operations in the other domain, which are sometimes easier to perform. The operation of [differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative) in the time domain corresponds to multiplication by the frequency,[[note 8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform#cite_note-78) so some [differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_equation) are easier to analyze in the frequency domain. Also, [convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution) in the time domain corresponds to ordinary multiplication in the frequency domain (see *[Convolution theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution_theorem)*). After performing the desired operations, transformation of the result can be made back to the time domain. [Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis) is the systematic study of the relationship between the frequency and time domains, including the kinds of functions or operations that are "simpler" in one or the other, and has deep connections to many areas of modern mathematics.

Analysis of differential equations

# Analysis of differential equations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fourier_transform&action=edit&section=48)]

Perhaps the most important use of the Fourier transformation is to solve [partial differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation). Many of the equations of the mathematical physics of the nineteenth century can be treated this way. Fourier studied the heat equation, which in one dimension and in dimensionless units is         ∂  2   y ( x , t )    ∂  2   x    =    ∂ y ( x , t )   ∂ t    .   {\displaystyle {\frac {\partial ^{2}y(x,t)}{\partial ^{2}x}}={\frac {\partial y(x,t)}{\partial t}}.}   The example we will give, a slightly more difficult one, is the wave equation in one dimension,         ∂  2   y ( x , t )    ∂  2   x    =     ∂  2   y ( x , t )    ∂  2   t    .   {\displaystyle {\frac {\partial ^{2}y(x,t)}{\partial ^{2}x}}={\frac {\partial ^{2}y(x,t)}{\partial ^{2}t}}.}

As usual, the problem is not to find a solution: there are infinitely many. The problem is that of the so-called "boundary problem": find a solution that satisfies the 'boundary conditions'     y ( x , 0 ) = f ( x ) ,     ∂ y ( x , 0 )   ∂ t    = g ( x ) .   {\displaystyle y(x,0)=f(x),\qquad {\frac {\partial y(x,0)}{\partial t}}=g(x).}

Here, f and g are given functions. For the heat equation, only one boundary condition can be required (usually the first one). But for the wave equation, there are still infinitely many solutions y that satisfy the first boundary condition. But when one imposes both conditions, there is only one possible solution.

It is easier to find the Fourier transform ŷ of the solution than to find the solution directly. This is because the Fourier transformation takes differentiation into multiplication by the Fourier-dual variable, and so a partial differential equation applied to the original function is transformed into multiplication by polynomial functions of the dual variables applied to the transformed function. After ŷ is determined, we can apply the inverse Fourier transformation to find y.

Fourier's method is as follows. First, note that any function of the forms     cos ⁡   (   2 π ξ ( x ± t )   )     or   sin ⁡   (   2 π ξ ( x ± t )   )     {\displaystyle \cos {\bigl (}2\pi \xi (x\pm t){\bigr )}{\text{ or }}\sin {\bigl (}2\pi \xi (x\pm t){\bigr )}}   satisfies the wave equation. These are called the elementary solutions.

Second, note that therefore any integral         y ( x , t ) =  ∫  0   ∞   d ξ   [      a  +   ( ξ ) cos ⁡   (   2 π ξ ( x + t )   )   +  a  −   ( ξ ) cos ⁡   (   2 π ξ ( x − t )   )   +         b  +   ( ξ ) sin ⁡   (   2 π ξ ( x + t )   )   +  b  −   ( ξ ) sin ⁡  (  2 π ξ ( x − t )  )    ]         {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}y(x,t)=\int _{0}^{\infty }d\xi {\Bigl [}&a_{+}(\xi )\cos {\bigl (}2\pi \xi (x+t){\bigr )}+a_{-}(\xi )\cos {\bigl (}2\pi \xi (x-t){\bigr )}+{}\\&b_{+}(\xi )\sin {\bigl (}2\pi \xi (x+t){\bigr )}+b_{-}(\xi )\sin \left(2\pi \xi (x-t)\right){\Bigr ]}\end{aligned}}}   satisfies the wave equation for arbitrary *a*+, *a*−, *b*+, *b*−. This integral may be interpreted as a continuous linear combination of solutions for the linear equation.

Now this resembles the formula for the Fourier synthesis of a function. In fact, this is the real inverse Fourier transform of *a*± and *b*± in the variable x.

The third step is to examine how to find the specific unknown coefficient functions *a*± and *b*± that will lead to y satisfying the boundary conditions. We are interested in the values of these solutions at *t* = 0. So we will set *t* = 0. Assuming that the conditions needed for Fourier inversion are satisfied, we can then find the Fourier sine and cosine transforms (in the variable x) of both sides and obtain     2  ∫  − ∞   ∞   y ( x , 0 ) cos ⁡ ( 2 π ξ x )  d x =  a  +   +  a  −     {\displaystyle 2\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }y(x,0)\cos(2\pi \xi x)\,dx=a_{+}+a_{-}}   and     2  ∫  − ∞   ∞   y ( x , 0 ) sin ⁡ ( 2 π ξ x )  d x =  b  +   +  b  −   .   {\displaystyle 2\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }y(x,0)\sin(2\pi \xi x)\,dx=b_{+}+b_{-}.}
